title: The old new commandment (1 John 2:1–11)
hook: whoever hates his brother walks in darkness

segments.voice: Yesterday: God is light, and confession, saying the same thing the light shows. Your line was faithful to forgive.

Is it old or new? The writer of First John can't seem to decide, and that's the point. Within two verses he says, I'm not writing you a new commandment, it's an old one. Then, right away: actually, it is new. It sounds like a man changing his mind mid-sentence. It isn't. Ask a couple married for decades: the same words, I love you, can be very old and brand new at once. Today, the commandment that is both.

He starts tenderly: "My little children, these things write I unto you, that ye sin not. And if any man sin, we have an advocate with the Father, Jesus Christ the righteous." An advocate stands beside you in court and speaks for you. Then a simple test: how do we know we know God? We keep his commandments, not just say we do. Then the riddle: "Brethren, I write no new commandment unto you, but an old commandment which ye had from the beginning." Which old commandment? Love. It runs back through the Torah: "love thy neighbour as thyself," in Leviticus. It's what his readers heard from the very beginning of their faith. Then he flips it: "Again, a new commandment I write unto you." New, because in John's Gospel, at the Last Supper, Jesus says, "A new commandment I give unto you, That ye love one another." New, because now it has a face: love as he loved. And new, the writer says, "because the darkness is past, and the true light now shineth." It's dawn: something old seen in fresh light. Then the hard edge: "He that saith he is in the light, and hateth his brother, is in darkness even until now." Whoever hates walks in darkness and doesn't know where he's going, because the darkness has blinded his eyes. Hatred doesn't only hurt the other person; it takes away your own sight. Love is how you see where you're going.
screen: then, large: `THE TRUE LIGHT NOW SHINETH.`

segments.voice: Think of someone you hold something against, a small irritation or an old hurt, and notice what happens in your chest as you picture them. Ask quietly what this grudge has kept you from seeing, about them, about you, about the way forward, without trying to fix it now. If you pray, pray for them by name.
Advocate. First John's name for Christ with the Father: someone who stands beside you in court and speaks for you when you sin.
Your line: walk in the light. An old command, in a new dawn. Day six hundred eighty-three, done.

howItsDone: Christians remember the new commandment especially on Maundy Thursday, whose name is usually traced to the Latin mandatum, commandment, and many churches read 1 John 2 when teaching about love within the community.

what a scholar hears: paraklētos, the advocate, used of Jesus here and of the Spirit in John's Gospel; and the new commandment of John 13:34 behind 'new'.

chat.says: Is 'love one another' an old rule or a new one? The letter says both.
options: Both: love is old, from the Torah, and new because Jesus gave it a face, love as he loved.
Old only: the writer just means the Ten Commandments, and there's nothing new in it.
It depends on the reader: old for the older believers, and new for the young ones.
chat.meaning: Love is the old command, from Leviticus. It's new because Jesus said love one another as he loved, and the true light now shines.

notes: Identification of the 'old commandment' with love (Leviticus 19:18 and the readers' first teaching) and the 'new' with John 13:34 is the common reading; confirm.
Maundy Thursday and Latin 'mandatum': standard derivation; confirm.
παράκλητος in 1 John 2:1 and John 14:16, 26: confirm.
